o: Has a duct that pierces masseter

The duct runs forward on the surface of masseter, then turns in to pierce buccinator.
It opens opposite the upper second molar.
Receives secretomotor fibres from the chorda tympani

Its secretomotor fibres come from IX via the lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve.
The chorda tympani supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Has a duct about 2 cm long

The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, like the submandibular duct.
It can be felt on a clenched masseter. (Last's p. 436)
Has the facial nerve as its most superficial major structure

Superficial to deep: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery.
Parotid tumours can therefore cause facial palsy.
Has a duct that passes below the lingual nerve

The lingual nerve loops under the duct, from lateral to medial.
So the duct lies above the nerve where they cross.
Has a duct about 5 cm long

The duct runs forward from the deep part to open beside the frenulum of the tongue.
It is the same length as the parotid duct. (Last's p. 436)
Is supplied by secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion

It is supplied through the submandibular ganglion, from VII via the chorda tympani.
The otic ganglion supplies the parotid.
Has a deep part lying on hyoglossus

The gland wraps round the back edge of mylohyoid; its deep part lies on hyoglossus.
The duct runs forward from it.
Vagus nerve

The vagus lies in the back of the sheath between artery and vein.
It runs the full length of the sheath.
Sympathetic trunk

The sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, on the prevertebral fascia.
It is not inside it.
Phrenic nerve

The phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior, deep to the prevertebral fascia.
It is well behind the sheath.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve

The recurrent laryngeal runs up in the groove between trachea and oesophagus.
That is medial to the sheath.

questions.s: Branches of the external carotid artery include the:
o: Superior thyroid artery

It is the first anterior branch, near the bifurcation.
It supplies the upper pole of the thyroid and the larynx.
Lingual artery

It loops up and passes deep to hyoglossus.
The hypoglossal nerve lies superficial to hyoglossus.
Facial artery

It grooves the submandibular gland and crosses the mandible at the front of masseter.
Its tonsillar branch is the main supply to the tonsil.
Ascending pharyngeal artery

It is the only medial branch, running up on the pharynx.
It also sends meningeal branches into the skull.
Has an isthmus over the fifth to seventh tracheal rings

The isthmus usually lies over the second to fourth rings.
A tracheostomy may need it divided or pushed aside.
Has an inferior thyroid artery from the external carotid

The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian.
The superior thyroid artery is from the external carotid.
Lies outside the pretracheal fascia

The pretracheal fascia encloses the gland and fixes it to the larynx.
So the thyroid moves up on swallowing.
Has a middle thyroid vein draining into the internal jugular vein

The short middle thyroid vein joins the internal jugular vein.
It must be tied early in thyroidectomy.
Is divided into three parts by scalenus anterior

The first part is medial, the second behind, the third lateral to the muscle.
The third part lies in the posterior triangle.
Gives the vertebral artery from its first part

The vertebral is the first branch, running up to C6.
It is the first branch on both sides.
Gives the thyrocervical trunk from its first part

The thyrocervical trunk arises at the medial edge of scalenus anterior.
It gives the inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries.
Has the trunks of the brachial plexus in front of its third part

The trunks lie above and behind the third part.
The lower trunk lies behind the artery on the first rib.
Enters the foramen transversarium of C7

It usually enters at C6.
C7's foramen transmits only veins. (Last's p. 555)
Enters the skull through the jugular foramen

It enters through the foramen magnum after piercing the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane.
Then it runs up in front of the medulla.
Joins its fellow at the upper border of the pons

The two vertebrals join at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
The basilar divides at the upper border into the posterior cerebrals.
Lies in a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas

After the atlas foramen it curves back in the groove on the posterior arch.
There it lies in the suboccipital triangle.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds

It rotates the arytenoids to open the rima glottidis.
Bilateral paralysis can block the airway.
Cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve

Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
It is the only intrinsic muscle not supplied by the recurrent.
The vocal folds are covered by ciliated columnar epithelium

The vocal folds have stratified squamous epithelium.
This resists wear from vibration.
Thyroarytenoid tenses and lengthens the vocal folds

Thyroarytenoid shortens and relaxes the folds.
Cricothyroid tenses and lengthens them.
Lies in the piriform fossa

It lies in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
The piriform fossa is in the laryngopharynx.
Has a bed formed by the superior constrictor

Superior constrictor forms the bed, with the glossopharyngeal nerve deep to it.
Damage to IX causes earache after tonsillectomy.
Is supplied mainly by the lingual artery

Its main supply is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.
It pierces the superior constrictor.
Has a paratonsillar vein that is the main source of bleeding after tonsillectomy

The paratonsillar (external palatine) vein runs down from the soft palate across the tonsil bed.
Bleeding after surgery is usually venous from here.
Levator palati is supplied by the mandibular nerve

Levator palati is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
Only tensor palati is supplied by V3.
Palatoglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve

Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
It is the one "tongue" muscle not supplied by XII.
Tensor palati is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus

Tensor palati is supplied by V3, through the nerve to medial pterygoid.
It hooks round the pterygoid hamulus. (Last's p. 633)
Musculus uvulae is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus

All palatal muscles except tensor palati are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
The motor fibres come from the vagus (cranial accessory).
Has articular surfaces covered by hyaline cartilage

They are covered by fibrocartilage.
The mandible and temporal bone ossify in membrane.
Has lateral pterygoid inserting only into the neck of the mandible

Lateral pterygoid inserts into the neck and also the disc and capsule.
So it pulls the disc forward on opening.
Is supplied only by the facial nerve

It is supplied by the auriculotemporal and masseteric nerves (V3).
Hilton's law applies.
Has a disc dividing it into upper and lower compartments

Gliding occurs in the upper compartment, hinge movement in the lower.
Opening the mouth wide needs both.
Masseter elevates the mandible

Masseter closes the jaw.
It is supplied by the masseteric nerve through the mandibular notch.
The posterior fibres of temporalis retract the mandible

The horizontal posterior fibres pull the mandible back.
The anterior fibres elevate.
Lateral pterygoid protrudes the mandible and opens the mouth

It pulls condyle and disc forward.
It is the only muscle of mastication that helps open the mouth.
Medial pterygoid elevates the mandible

It runs parallel to masseter on the inside of the ramus.
The two together form a sling.
Superior oblique is tested by asking the patient to look down and in

In adduction superior oblique is the main depressor.
So a IV palsy gives difficulty going downstairs.
Lateral rectus is supplied by the trochlear nerve

Lateral rectus is supplied by VI (LR6 SO4).
IV supplies only superior oblique.
Inferior oblique arises from the back of the orbit

It arises from the floor of the orbit near the front, just lateral to the nasolacrimal canal.
It is the only extraocular muscle not arising from the back.
Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied only by sympathetic fibres

The striated part is supplied by III; only its smooth part (superior tarsal) is sympathetic.
So III palsy gives complete ptosis, Horner's only partial.
Has the promontory on its lateral wall

The promontory, made by the basal turn of the cochlea, is on the medial wall.
The tympanic membrane forms most of the lateral wall.
Has the tegmen tympani as its roof

The tegmen tympani separates it from the middle cranial fossa.
Infection can spread up to the temporal lobe.
Has the internal carotid artery related to its posterior wall

The internal carotid is related to the anterior wall.
The aditus to the antrum is on the posterior wall.
Has the aditus to the mastoid antrum on its posterior wall

The aditus opens from the epitympanic recess into the antrum.
The facial canal lies below it.
Has its outer surface supplied only by the vagus

The outer surface is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve and the auricular branch of the vagus.
The inner surface is supplied by IX.
Has its pars flaccida below the handle of the malleus

The pars flaccida lies above the lateral process of the malleus.
The chorda tympani crosses it.
Faces directly laterally

It faces laterally, forwards and downwards.
So the meatus must be straightened to see it.
Has the handle of the malleus attached to its inner surface

The handle is attached down to the umbo.
The light reflex runs anteroinferiorly from the umbo.
Has loose areolar tissue as its "dangerous" layer

Blood and pus spread easily in this layer, and emissary veins cross it.
It allows the scalp to move over the pericranium.
Has its vessels in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue

Vessels in this layer are held open, so scalp wounds bleed freely.
This is why a scalp laceration bleeds so much.
Has the galea aponeurotica joining frontalis and occipitalis

The aponeurosis is the tendon of occipitofrontalis.
A wound through it gapes.
Has no sensory supply from cervical nerves

The back of the scalp is supplied by the greater occipital (C2) and lesser occipital (C2) nerves.
The front is supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
Has a superior cervical ganglion formed by fusion of the ganglia for C1–4

The superior cervical ganglion lies opposite C1 and C2.
It gives grey rami to C1–4.
Lies within the carotid sheath

It lies behind the sheath on the prevertebral fascia.
So it is not inside the sheath.
Has a middle cervical ganglion at the level of C3

The middle cervical ganglion lies at C6, near the inferior thyroid artery.
It is often small or absent.
Gives white rami to the cervical nerves

Cervical nerves receive only grey rami.
White rami arise only from T1 to L2.

questions.s: A lesion of the cervical sympathetic trunk produces:
o: A dilated pupil

The pupil is small (miosis), as dilator pupillae loses its supply.
The light reflex is preserved.
Complete ptosis

Ptosis is partial, from paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle.
Complete ptosis suggests III palsy.
Facial weakness on the same side

Facial muscles are supplied by VII, not by sympathetic fibres.
Horner's syndrome does not cause facial weakness.
Loss of sweating on the same side of the face

Anhidrosis follows if the lesion is below the superior cervical ganglion.
Sweat glands get sympathetic fibres along the external carotid branches.
Has a nasolacrimal duct opening into the middle meatus

The duct opens into the inferior meatus.
A valve-like fold guards its opening.
Has a lacrimal sac in a fossa formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of maxilla

The sac lies in this fossa behind the medial palpebral ligament.
It continues down as the nasolacrimal duct.
Has a gland supplied by secretomotor fibres from the chorda tympani

Lacrimal secretomotor fibres come from VII through the greater petrosal and pterygopalatine ganglion.
The chorda tympani supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Has a palpebral part seen in the lateral upper conjunctival fornix

The gland's palpebral part lies below levator's aponeurosis.
Its ducts open into the upper lateral fornix.
All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve

XII supplies all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles.
A lesion makes the tongue deviate to the weak side on protrusion.
Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus

Palatoglossus is the exception among the tongue muscles.
It is really a palatal muscle.
General sensation from the anterior two-thirds is carried by the lingual nerve

The lingual nerve (V3) carries general sensation.
Taste from this part runs in the chorda tympani.
The posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve

IX carries both general sensation and taste from the posterior third.
The internal laryngeal supplies the area near the epiglottis.
